output.headline: Fonagy review sets out scale of ADHD and autism demand facing NHS
output.standfirst: A government-commissioned review by Prof Peter Fonagy sets out the scale of demand for ADHD, autism and mental health care, after finding the NHS risks ‘system failures’ with more than 800,000 people waiting for assessment.
output.bodyHtml:
The NHS in England should move to a “needs-led” system for mental health, ADHD and autism care, a government-commissioned review has concluded, after finding that the health service is heading into a “world of system failures” as it struggles to cope with demand that has left more than 800,000 people waiting for an ADHD or autism assessment, some of them desperate for support.

The review said patients’ needs meant the NHS should bring together mental health and neurodevelopmental services and move to a “needs-led” system.

The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health backed Fonagy’s call for diagnosis to no longer dictate who receives care.

Dr Ronny Cheung, the college’s officer for health services, said: “Too often, a diagnosis is the only route to accessing meaningful help. This means that children and families can be left struggling alone while waiting for assessments, with little or no support available in the meantime.”

Moving to a “needs-led” approach would “ensure children and young people can seamlessly and more quickly access a robust, holistic and reliable standard of care”, he added.

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, will draw on Fonagy’s recommendations as she puts together the forthcoming mental health strategy, due by the end of the year.

In her response, Cooper promised that the NHS would provide a “needs-led” system under which people would get much faster care, and she has asked NHS England to establish how it can provide faster advice, assessments and treatment.

She said: “It is clear that mental health services need to change to focus more on the early support young people need to stay in education or work or keep their lives on track.”

She also pledged to ensure all private assessment clinics are regulated, though she did not commit to the advertising ban Fonagy said was needed.

Prof Peter Fonagy led the review, which examined the sharp rise in demand over recent decades for help with mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions and produced the warning of system failures.

It urged ministers to toughen regulation of the private clinics that many people turn to because they cannot get assessed quickly by the NHS, while warning of an increasing risk of overdiagnosis of autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

The experts behind the review also called for access to care to be based primarily on a person’s needs so fewer people would have years-long waits for a formal diagnosis.

Related: NHS England mental health services review: what has it found and what does it recommend?

The review found that the number of people suffering mental distress has risen significantly across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially the under-18s.

The number of 16- to 64-year-olds with a common mental disorder increased from 15.5 per cent in 1993 to 22.6 per cent in 2024. However, it jumped more sharply – from about one in six to one in four – among 16- to 24-year-olds over the same period.

The report, which runs to 607 pages, found that the evidence shows sceptics are wrong to cast doubt on young people’s struggles.

“That’s sometimes been attributed to personal failures, people being told they’re making it up, it’s all in their head, which is absolute nonsense,” said Prof Simon Wessely, a leading psychiatrist and vice-chair of the review.

The findings may have significant implications for the government’s drive to reduce the number of young people in the UK not in education, employment or training – now almost 1 million – and the size of the welfare bill, with a record 2.8 million people too sick to work; and also for schools as they grapple with the demands arising from the growing number of pupils with special educational needs.

Fonagy, a psychoanalyst and clinical psychologist at University College London, dismissed the notion that young people in particular were “snowflakes” who were less resilient than in previous generations. “The rise in mental health problems is real, is affecting everyday functioning and cannot be explained by greater awareness alone,” his report said.

He said an array of social and economic circumstances had piled unprecedented pressure on young people. “There is increased uncertainty – financial pressures, insecure work, unaffordable housing – but perhaps more important, a lack of hope among young people that their lives will be better than their parents, and that’s the first time since the second world war that surveys have noticed that.”

Fonagy said the explosion in demand for help with mental ill-health and neurodiversity had left people stuck on waiting lists for years at a time and with worsening symptoms. At the end of last year more than 560,000 people in England were waiting to be assessed for ADHD – 17 times more than in 2019 – and another 254,000 were waiting for a diagnostic assessment for autism, taking the total waiting to more than 800,000, almost all of them – 90 per cent – for at least three months.

The number of six- to 11-year-olds diagnosed with autism has also soared, jumping 20-fold to 4.58 per cent between 2000 and 2025, and by even more among those aged 12 to 17 over the same years – from 0.1 per cent to 4.06 per cent, a 40-fold rise. The proportion of six- to 11-year-olds with an ADHD diagnosis has increased more than sixfold in five years, and more than 15-fold among 12- to 17-year-olds, to 2.7 per cent and 3.9 per cent respectively.

The report warned that if current trends continue, the 4 million children who already suffer “high psychological distress” could become 4.5 million by 2030, with the number of under-18s who self-harm rising from 1.9 million to 2.5 million.

Wessely warned that the exponential rise in diagnoses of autism and ADHD means the UK has reached a “tipping point” where people are at risk of being misdiagnosed with either condition.

The authors did not find that overdiagnosis was occurring at scale, but added that the evidence “suggests we are entering a phase in which the balance of risks between underdiagnosis, misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis may be changing, with the risks of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis becoming increasingly important considerations for policy and service delivery”.

The increasing tendency of young people to self-identify as neurodivergent – as many as a fifth of secondary school pupils do so – means that “the line between the social and the medical is beginning to blur”, they added.

The 10-month review found “strong concerns about the consistency and quality of ADHD and autism assessments being carried out by independent providers, and the financial incentives associated with assessment activity”.

Ministers should ban direct-to-public advertising of such services and ensure that all clinics offering them are regulated by the Care Quality Commission, it said.

Growing numbers of young people have a combination of mental ill-health and ADHD or autism, or both. “Co-occurence is the rule rather than the exception,” the report said. For example, 61 per cent of 16- to 24-year-olds with a common mental health condition also had autistic traits, and 57 per cent had ADHD symptoms.
output.progress: Yvette Cooper has asked NHS England to find ways to provide faster assessments and treatment, drawing on the review for her mental health strategy.
